claim: The currently recommended dose of tafenoquine (300 mg in adults, average dose of 5 mg/kg) is insufficient for cure in all adults.
source: We concluded that the currently recommended dose of tafenoquine (300 mg in adults, average dose of 5 mg/kg) is insufficient for cure in all adults
evidence: Based on individual patient pharmacometric data meta-analysis from tafenoquine pre-registration clinical efficacy trials

claim: A 50% increase in tafenoquine dose to 450 mg (7.5 mg/kg) would halve the risk of vivax recurrence by four months.
source: a 50% increase to 450 mg (7.5 mg/kg) would halve the risk of vivax recurrence by four months
evidence: Based on pharmacometric modeling from individual patient data meta-analysis

claim: Clinical trials of higher tafenoquine doses should be carried out to assess their safety and tolerability.
source: We recommended that clinical trials of higher doses should be carried out to assess their safety and tolerability.
evidence: Recommendation based on efficacy analysis showing suboptimal dosing

claim: The relative haemolytic risks of the 300 mg and 450 mg tafenoquine doses have not been sufficiently well characterised.
source: We contend that the relative haemolytic risks of the 300 mg and 450 mg doses have not been sufficiently well characterised to justify this opinion.
evidence: Assessment of available safety data in the literature

claim: Most antimalarial drugs have required dose optimisation following their initial introduction.
source: Most antimalarial drugs have required dose optimisation following their initial introduction.
evidence: General statement about antimalarial drug development history

claim: Tafenoquine is likely not an exception to requiring dose optimisation.
source: It appears likely that tafenoquine is not an exception.
evidence: Inference based on general antimalarial drug development patterns and current efficacy data

claim: The dose-response relationship for tafenoquine-induced haemolysis in G6PD deficiency has not been well characterised.
source: The dose-response relationship for tafenoquine-induced haemolysis in G6PD deficiency has not been well characterised
evidence: Assessment of available safety data from clinical trials

claim: The entirety of the available data for the 300 mg tafenoquine dose comprises 3 heterozygous females with >40% enzyme activity.
source: the entirety of the available data for the 300 mg dose comprises 3 heterozygous females with >40% enzyme activity, Rueangweerayut et al., 2017
evidence: Referenced from Rueangweerayut et al., 2017 study

claim: Tafenoquine is restricted to patients with G6PD activity >70%.
source: which is why the drug is restricted to patients with G6PD activity >70%
evidence: Statement about current regulatory/clinical guidelines

claim: Tafenoquine, if not used appropriately, may have a higher risk of causing severe haemolysis compared with primaquine.
source: Compared with primaquine, the most widely used 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial, tafenoquine, if not used appropriately, may have a higher risk of causing severe haemolysis.
evidence: Comparison based on pharmacological properties and clinical knowledge

claim: Primaquine can be stopped once haemolysis is apparent, and the effect is short-lived.
source: Primaquine can be stopped once haemolysis is apparent, and the effect is short-lived.
evidence: Based on known pharmacological properties of primaquine

claim: Tafenoquine has an elimination half-life of approximately 16 days.
source: Tafenoquine has an elimination half-life of approximately 16 days
evidence: Pharmacokinetic data from clinical studies

claim: Tafenoquine cannot be stopped once administered.
source: Tafenoquine has an elimination half-life of approximately 16 days and cannot be "stopped".
evidence: Inference from long elimination half-life

claim: High doses (up to 15 mg/kg) of tafenoquine are well tolerated in G6PD normal individuals.
source: As high doses (up to 15 mg/kg) of tafenoquine are well tolerated in G6PD normal individuals (the substantial majority of patients, Watson et al., 2022)
evidence: Referenced from Watson et al., 2022 analysis

claim: Prevention of relapse provides substantial health benefits.
source: prevention of relapse provides substantial health benefits (Dini et al., 2020)
evidence: Referenced from Dini et al., 2020

claim: In the DETECTIVE study, only 57 patients received 300 mg and 56 received 600 mg tafenoquine, distributed across four different countries.
source: Only 57 patients received 300 mg and 56 received 600 mg, distributed across four different countries.
evidence: Data from DETECTIVE phase 2 trial

claim: One of the countries in the DETECTIVE study was India where long latency relapse strains are found.
source: One of the countries was India where long latency relapse strains are found.
evidence: Geographic and epidemiological knowledge about P. vivax strains

claim: Long latency relapses would have occurred after 6 months (the DETECTIVE study's follow up duration).
source: These relapses would have occurred after 6 months (the study's follow up duration).
evidence: Inference based on known relapse patterns of long latency strains

claim: The odds ratio for any recurrence at 6 months in the DETECTIVE phase 2 trial is 0.67 per mg/kg increase (95% CI 0.58–0.76).
source: We estimate an odds ratio for any recurrence at 6 months of 0.67 per mg/kg increase (95% CI 0.58–0.76).
evidence: Logistic regression model fitted to DETECTIVE phase 2 efficacy data

claim: At 4 months, the odds ratio for recurrence in the DETECTIVE phase 2 trial is 0.62 (95% CI 0.51–0.72) per mg/kg increase.
source: At 4 months this odds ratio is 0.62 (95% CI 0.51–0.72)
evidence: Logistic regression model fitted to DETECTIVE phase 2 efficacy data

claim: The odds ratio for recurrence at 4 months in the DETECTIVE phase 2 trial is almost identical to results from the pooled dataset.
source: At 4 months this odds ratio is 0.62 (95% CI 0.51–0.72), i.e. almost identical to our results from the pooled dataset (Watson et al., 2022).
evidence: Comparison of DETECTIVE results with pooled meta-analysis results

claim: There have been no regulatory studies of primaquine.
source: We note that there have been no regulatory studies of primaquine.
evidence: Knowledge of primaquine development history

claim: A primaquine total dose of 7 mg/kg is approved by WHO for the Southeast Asian region.
source: A primaquine total dose of 7 mg/kg is approved by WHO for the Southeast Asian region.
evidence: WHO guidelines and recommendations

claim: A pooled individual patient data meta-analysis shows that primaquine 7 mg/kg dose is clearly more efficacious than 3.5 mg/kg.
source: A pooled individual patient data meta-analysis shows that this dose is clearly more efficacious than 3.5 mg/kg (Commons et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from Commons et al., 2023 meta-analysis

claim: The code for the statistical analysis is openly accessible.
source: The code for the statistical analysis is openly accessible.
evidence: Statement about data availability

claim: The terminal elimination half-life is not correlated with the mg/kg dose.
source: whereas the terminal elimination half-life is not
evidence: Pharmacokinetic analysis from the meta-analysis dataset

claim: When adjusting for the mg/kg dose, there was no longer a clear relationship between AUC and the odds of recurrence (95% CI for the adjusted odds ratio is 0.64–1.23).
source: When adjusting for the mg/kg dose, there was no longer a clear relationship between AUC and the odds of recurrence (95% CI for the adjusted odds ratio is 0.64–1.23)
evidence: Statistical analysis adjusting for dose in the meta-analysis

claim: In most tropical regions P. vivax relapses are highly predictable and occur within a few weeks to months after initial treatment.
source: In most tropical regions P. vivax relapses are highly predictable and occur within a few weeks to months after initial treatment.
evidence: Established knowledge about P. vivax relapse patterns

claim: Trials which have included no 8-aminoquinoline treatment arms indicate that >90% of first relapses occur within four months.
source: Trials which have included no 8-aminoquinoline treatment arms indicate that >90% of first relapses occur within four months (Commons et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from Commons et al., 2023 analysis

claim: Longer follow-up increases sensitivity (more relapses included) but lowers specificity (more reinfections included).
source: Longer follow-up increases sensitivity (more relapses included) but lowers specificity (more reinfections included).
evidence: Methodological reasoning about study design trade-offs

claim: The results of the analysis are almost identical when a 6 month endpoint was applied.
source: The results of our analysis are almost identical when a 6 month endpoint was applied. This was shown in Appendix 1—figures 4 and 5 in Watson et al., 2022.
evidence: Sensitivity analysis presented in Watson et al., 2022

claim: The mean tafenoquine dose in the TEACH study was approximately 7.0 mg/kg.
source: Using the reported mean body weights (Table 1 in Vélez et al., 2022), the mean dose was approximately 7.0 mg/kg.
evidence: Calculation based on data from Vélez et al., 2022

claim: In the INSPECTOR study, the failure rate was 67% in patients weighing ≤69kg.
source: The failure rate was 67% in the patients weighing ≤69kg
evidence: Data from INSPECTOR study (Sutanto et al., 2023)

claim: In the INSPECTOR study, the failure rate was 91% in patients weighing >69 kg.
source: but was 91% in the patients weighing >69 kg
evidence: Data from INSPECTOR study (Sutanto et al., 2023)

claim: In the INSPECTOR study, the odds ratio for failure is 5.3 (95%CI 1.0–27.5; P=0.07) comparing higher to lower weight patients.
source: odds ratio for failure is 5.3 [95%CI 1.0–27.5; P=0.07]
evidence: Statistical analysis of INSPECTOR study data

claim: Tafenoquine and primaquine cause increases in blood methaemoglobin.
source: The observation that tafenoquine and primaquine cause increases in blood methaemoglobin is uncontroversial.
evidence: Established pharmacological knowledge

claim: A recent analysis of different 8-aminoquinoline studies conducted over the past 80 years shows a clear relationship between radical curative efficacy and methaemoglobinaemia.
source: A recent analysis of different 8-aminoquinoline studies conducted over the past 80 years shows a clear relationship between radical curative efficacy and methaemoglobinaemia (White et al., 2022).
evidence: Referenced from White et al., 2022 analysis

claim: The gametocytocidal and hypnozoitocidal activities of primaquine result from the generation of reactive intermediates.
source: There is also general agreement that the gametocytocidal and hypnozoitocidal activities of tafenoquine's predecessor primaquine result from the generation of reactive intermediates.
evidence: Established scientific consensus about primaquine mechanism

claim: Tafenoquine clinical trial data show that greater methaemoglobin values on day 7 are correlated with a lower probability of recurrence at 4 months (after adjustment for the mg/kg dose).
source: Tafenoquine clinical trial data show that greater methaemoglobin values on day 7 are correlated with a lower probability of recurrence at 4 months (after adjustment for the mg/kg dose, Watson et al., 2022).
evidence: Analysis from Watson et al., 2022

claim: The relationship between methaemoglobin and recurrence observed for tafenoquine is the same as observed for primaquine and pamaquine (plasmoquine).
source: This is the same relationship observed for primaquine and pamaquine (plasmoquine), suggesting these structurally related compounds all share a common mode of action.
evidence: Comparison across different 8-aminoquinoline drugs

claim: The hypothesis that methaemoglobin is a biomarker of efficacy was prespecified before the tafenoquine meta-analysis.
source: Importantly this hypothesis was prespecified before the tafenoquine meta-analysis (White et al., 2022).
evidence: Referenced from White et al., 2022

claim: Each additional mg/kg of tafenoquine was associated with a 19% (95% CI: 17% to 21%) increase in day 7 MetHb concentrations.
source: Each additional mg/kg was associated with a 19% (95% CI: 17% to 21%) increase in day 7 MetHb concentrations
evidence: Linear model analysis from the meta-analysis dataset

claim: Under the Gini criterion, the optimal split for a continuous covariate with a continuous relationship with the outcome is the value which equally balances sensitivity and specificity.
source: Under the Gini criterion the cut-off threshold is the value which equally balances sensitivity and specificity for a continuous covariate which has a continuous relationship with the outcome (e.g. a linear relationship on the log-odds scale).
evidence: Statistical methodology knowledge about CART models

claim: TEACH was a single arm, non-randomised study with no control group.
source: Firstly, we note that TEACH was a single arm, non-randomised study with no control group.
evidence: Study design information from TEACH trial

claim: There are two discrete sequential risk distributions for G6PD deficient patients receiving tafenoquine, neither of which have been well characterised.
source: There are two discrete sequential risk distributions for these G6PD deficient patients, neither of which have been well characterised.
evidence: Assessment of available safety data and testing procedures

claim: No G6PD deficient patient should receive tafenoquine with current quantitative testing.
source: No G6PD deficient patient should receive tafenoquine with current quantitative testing.
evidence: Clinical guideline and safety recommendation

claim: There are no available data on how frequently G6PD testing mistakes will occur.
source: There are no available data on how frequently testing mistakes will occur.
evidence: Assessment of available literature on testing accuracy

claim: There is no evidence to compare the haemolytic risks between the 5 mg/kg and 7.5 mg/kg tafenoquine doses in G6PD deficient patients.
source: We also have no evidence to compare the subsequent haemolytic risks between the 5 mg/kg and 7.5 mg/kg doses.
evidence: Assessment of available safety data

claim: The individual patient data pharmacometric meta-analysis provides an evidence-based characterisation of the dose-response relationship for radical curative efficacy in vivax malaria.
source: The individual patient data pharmacometric meta-analysis of the tafenoquine pre-registration studies provides an evidence-based characterisation of the dose-response relationship for radical curative efficacy in vivax malaria.
evidence: Summary of the meta-analysis findings

claim: When using the current 5 mg/kg tafenoquine regimen, a substantial proportion of adults will be under-dosed.
source: The results demonstrate clearly that when using the current 5 mg/kg regimen a substantial proportion of adults will be under-dosed
evidence: Inference from dose-response analysis

claim: There would be a substantial benefit from increasing the tafenoquine dose to 7.5 mg/kg.
source: and therefore that there would be a substantial benefit from increasing the dose to 7.5 mg/kg
evidence: Inference from dose-response analysis

claim: The relative haemolytic risks for the 5 mg/kg and 7.5 mg/kg tafenoquine doses are not known.
source: In this scenario the relative haemolytic risks for the 5 mg/kg and 7.5 mg/kg are not known.
evidence: Assessment of available safety data

claim: The development and regulatory approval of tafenoquine has provided a critical alternative for vivax radical cure in endemic countries.
source: The development and regulatory approval of tafenoquine has provided a critical alternative for vivax radical cure in endemic countries.
evidence: Knowledge of tafenoquine's role in malaria treatment

claim: Further prospective clinical trials of higher tafenoquine doses are needed to characterise their efficacy, safety and tolerability.
source: Our analysis supports the need for further prospective clinical trials of higher tafenoquine doses to characterise their efficacy, safety and tolerability.
evidence: Recommendation based on meta-analysis findings
